## What each known task tells us

**Y components.** Only one bit position explains each task.
- Y3 is bit 1. In X2-Y3-Z2, the answer is 0 exactly when the two bit-1 values differ.
- Y1 is bit 4. In X4-Y1-Z1, the answer is 3 exactly when both bit-4 values are 0.
- Y2 is bit 3. In X2-Y2-Z1 and X3-Y2-Z4, bit 3 is the only position that fits.

**X and Z components.** Each task fixes only a pair (rule, button mapping). Swapping a rule for its complement and flipping the Z mapping gives the same behaviour.

| Task | Option A | Option B |
|---|---|---|
| X2-Y3-Z2 | X2 = same, Z2: T→2 F→0 | X2 = exactly one, Z2: T→0 F→2 |
| X4-Y3-Z2 | X4 = neither (with Z2 T→2) | X4 = at least one (with Z2 T→0) |
| X2-Y2-Z1 | X2 = same, Z1: T→3 F→2 | X2 = exactly one, Z1: T→2 F→3 |
| X4-Y1-Z1 | Agrees with the X4/Z1 choice in the same column | Agrees with the X4/Z1 choice in the same column |
| X3-Y3-Z3 | X3 = both, Z3: T→2 F→1 | X3 = not both, Z3: T→1 F→2 |
| X3-Y2-Z4 | X3 = both, Z4: T→1 F→2 | X3 = not both, Z4: T→2 F→1 |

The tasks link these choices into two independent groups:
- **H:** X2, X4, Z1 and Z2 either all take option A or all take option B.
- **K:** X3, Z3 and Z4 either all take option A or all take option B.

Every one of the 4 combinations fits all the examples, and all of them keep the X versions distinct.

## Consequence for X2-Y1-Z4 (bit 4)

- If H and K both take option A, or both take option B: same bit-4 values → **1**, different → **2**.
- If one takes A and the other takes B: same → **2**, different → **1**.

So the examples do not determine the answers. Two opposite answer sets are possible.

## Choosing between them

I looked for a cross-component pattern, such as "true always maps to the higher button". None holds consistently in any of the four combinations, so nothing settles the choice.

I lean slightly toward reading every component as option A. That uses the rules "same", "neither" and "both", and gives same → 1, different → 2. This preference is weak.

## Predictions

Applying same → 1, different → 2 to the bit-4 values of each input:

| # | Input | Bit 4 values | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0110 1000 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 0100 1101 | 0, 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 0110 0110 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1111 0011 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 5 | 1001 0000 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 6 | 1011 1110 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 7 | 1000 1001 | 0, 1 | 2 |
| 8 | 0001 0100 | 1, 0 | 2 |
| 9 | 1100 0100 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 10 | 0001 0101 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 11 | 0101 0001 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 12 | 1100 1110 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 13 | 0110 0100 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 14 | 0101 1011 | 1, 1 | 1 |
| 15 | 1110 0010 | 0, 0 | 1 |
| 16 | 0000 0011 | 0, 1 | 2 |

My confidence is about 0.5, since the two answer sets are equally consistent with the examples.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
